clue.text: Wordsworth, in certain circumstances, would have rather been one

definitions.text: Wordsworth, in certain circumstances, would have rather been one

parts.words: Wordsworth, in certain circumstances, would have rather been one
parts.note: alludes to Wordsworth's sonnet 'The world is too much with us', where he says he would rather be a heathen suckled in a creed outworn

explanation.surface: A literary teaser about what the poet Wordsworth once wished he could be.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue leans on the line 'Great God! I'd rather be a ... suckled in a creed outworn', with the answer being the missing word.
explanation.definitionFit: In the sonnet the poet wishes to be a heathen worshipper of nature, which is what the word means.

clue.text: He has nothing to sell to the wideawake

definitions.text: He has nothing to sell to the wideawake

parts.words: He has nothing to sell to the wideawake
parts.note: a hawker whose wares are sleepers' visions has no customers among people who are awake

explanation.surface: A street trader with no market among alert, sharp customers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wideawake' suggests shrewd buyers, but it means literally not asleep: this seller deals in visions of the night, as in Beddoes's poem 'Dream-Pedlary'.
explanation.definitionFit: A seller of sleepers' visions finds no trade among people who are not sleeping, hence the hawker of night visions.

clue.text: Likely trifling malady in a mucilage factory

definitions.text: Likely trifling malady in a mucilage factory

parts.words: Likely trifling malady in a mucilage factory
parts.note: a factory making mucilage (glue) would boil gum, and an abscess on the mouth's tissue is a minor ailment

explanation.surface: A joking guess at the occupational illness of workers in a glue works.
explanation.walkthrough: Mucilage is gum or glue; a factory making it would be boiling gum, and the minor ailment of that name is an abscess in the mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a small abscess on the tissue around a tooth, a trifling complaint, and also literally gum being boiled.

clue.text: Invalid

parts.note: as an adjective, having no legal force, as a contract declared void

explanation.walkthrough: The one-word clue tempts a reading of 'invalid' as a sick person; it is the adjective meaning void.
explanation.definitionFit: Something legally void has no force at all, the sense of the answer in the phrase 'null and void'.

clue.text: Their meetings made June " (Tennyson)

parts.note: a quotation from Tennyson's In Memoriam with a word missing, 'And their meetings made ... June', which the solver supplies

explanation.surface: A line of Tennyson with one word blanked out for the solver to supply.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed ditto mark stands for the gap: the full line from In Memoriam reads 'their meetings made December June', winter turned to summer.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word in the quoted line is the last month of the year, which their meetings turned into summer.

clue.text: Many a housewife has had a brush with them

definitions.text: Many a housewife has had a brush with them

parts.words: Many a housewife has had a brush with them
parts.note: a 'brush with' sounds like a quarrel, but literally a brush is used with these sweeping aids

explanation.surface: Housewives having run-ins or confrontations with some unnamed foe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Had a brush with' suggests a skirmish; the brush is the domestic sweeping kind, paired with a pan to collect dirt.
explanation.definitionFit: These shallow pans are always used together with a hand brush when sweeping up.

clue.text: Gap, Ivy, act to fill it

indicators.note: the words ivy and act are reworked into a new shape that fills the gap

explanation.surface: Ivy and an action are recommended for plugging a hole.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of IVY and ACT are rearranged; 'to fill it' signals that the reshuffled letters make the gap itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A hollow space or hole is a gap, the everyday sense of the answer.

clue.text: Comus " until altered into something else

indicators.note: the words Comus and until are changed into a fresh arrangement of the same letters

explanation.surface: Milton's masque Comus being adapted into a different work.
explanation.walkthrough: COMUS and UNTIL are rearranged together; the printed ditto mark is a stray in the newspaper. The definition is just 'something else', a teasing nod to an obscure word for a small mound or hillock.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a rare anatomical and geological term for a little hill, truly another thing entirely.

clue.text: Saved the bacon ? Well, it hasn't gone West

definitions.text: Saved the bacon ? Well, it hasn't gone West

parts.words: Saved the bacon ? Well, it hasn't gone West
parts.note: pork that has been saved has not 'gone west' (perished), so it has gone the other way, giving a London district name

explanation.surface: Someone rescued from disaster, with a quip that it didn't go fatally wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gone west' is slang for died or got lost. Meat that hasn't gone west has gone the opposite direction: an eastern joint, which is the name of a district of east London.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is a district of east London, and read literally it is a joint of pork pointing away from the west.

clue.text: One may get away with it, but not deliver the goods

definitions.text: One may get away with it, but not deliver the goods

parts.words: One may get away with it, but not deliver the goods
parts.note: you can travel off on it, but it carries people, not freight

explanation.surface: A sly person escaping blame yet failing to perform.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get away with it' and 'deliver the goods' read as idioms for evading blame and succeeding; literally they mean departing by it and hauling freight.
explanation.definitionFit: A railway service for people rather than freight takes travellers away but never carries cargo.

clue.text: Not such depressing depressions

parts.note: small hollows in cheeks are physical depressions, but charming rather than gloomy

explanation.surface: A cheerful remark that some low spells are less gloomy than others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Depressions' suggests low moods; here it means small hollows in the skin, which are attractive.
explanation.definitionFit: The small hollows in a cheek or chin when smiling are literal hollows in the skin, and pleasing ones.

clue.text: Swift's Esther

parts.note: Jonathan Swift gave Esther Vanhomrigh a coined pet name in his poem 'Cadenus and ...'

explanation.walkthrough: Swift invented the name from Esther Vanhomrigh's surname and first name, and used it in his poem 'Cadenus and Vanessa'.
explanation.definitionFit: Swift coined this name for his friend Esther Vanhomrigh by joining parts of her surname and given name.

clue.text: A turn for November, very wet

indicators.note: a turn here means the abbreviation for the eleventh month is read backwards

explanation.surface: A shift to rainy weather as autumn becomes November.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very wet' is a jokey definition: the name itself comes from the Celtic word for a river.
explanation.definitionFit: The name is that of several English rivers, and a river is about as wet as anything gets.

clue.text: It was the warden's job to do so at night

definitions.text: It was the warden's job to do so at night

parts.words: It was the warden's job to do so at night
parts.note: wartime air-raid wardens had to notice lamps showing during the blackout

explanation.surface: A wartime warden's night-time duty, described vaguely.
explanation.walkthrough: Air-raid precautions wardens in Britain's wartime blackout patrolled at night looking for any lamps left showing; the answer read as a phrase is that duty, and also names theatre lamps.
explanation.definitionFit: Read as two words it is the blackout warden's task of noticing visible lamps; as one word, strong stage lamps.

clue.text: It's most offensive!

parts.note: sounds like an outraged complaint, but means it is the most attacking thing

explanation.surface: An indignant cry at something rude.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Offensive' reads as insulting; it means attacking, as in a military offensive.
explanation.definitionFit: Hostile attacking behaviour is the very essence of being on the offensive.

clue.text: Gib lingo (anag.)

indicators.note: the printed abbreviation instructs the solver to rearrange the letters of the words before it

explanation.surface: Talk in the slang of Gibraltar, offered as a plain jumble.
explanation.walkthrough: An old-style clue with no definition at all: the solver rearranges GIB LINGO and relies on crossing letters to pick the right word.
explanation.definitionFit: No definition is printed; the rearranged result means helpful and willing to do a favour.

clue.text: The plant seems to be almost on the way

indicators.note: seems here means sounds like, the spoken form matching the plant's name

parts.note: on the way means coming, and almost drops its last letter, leaving comin'

explanation.surface: Someone thinks a plant is nearly arriving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' drops the G from COMING, leaving COMIN, and 'seems to be' says that spoken it matches the plant's name.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an old spelling of cumin, an aromatic plant whose seeds are used as a spice.

clue.text: Torn rose (anag.)

indicators.note: the printed abbreviation instructs the solver to rearrange the letters of the words before it

explanation.surface: A damaged flower, offered as a plain jumble.
explanation.walkthrough: An old-style clue with no definition at all: rearrange TORN ROSE and confirm with the crossing letters.
explanation.definitionFit: No definition is printed; the rearranged result is a resort town on the Bay of Naples in Italy.

clue.text: Reasons for going under ?

parts.note: sounds like several causes of failure, but literally people under water make the reason someone goes beneath the surface

explanation.surface: A query about why a business has failed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going under' suggests collapse; read literally it is going below water. The answer also means 'various', so it can stand for several reasons.
explanation.definitionFit: Underwater swimmers go below the surface, and as an old adjective the word means several or sundry.

clue.text: " A foul and pestilent congregation of" (Hamlet)

definitions.text: " A foul and pestilent congregation of" (Hamlet)

parts.words: " A foul and pestilent congregation of" (Hamlet)
parts.note: Hamlet calls the sky 'a foul and pestilent congregation of ...' — the missing word is supplied by the solver

explanation.surface: A quotation from Hamlet with its last word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: In Act 2 Hamlet says the heavens appear to him as 'a foul and pestilent congregation of' mists and exhalations; the missing last word is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word of Hamlet's speech means mists or exhalations, the gloomy air he sees overhead.

clue.text: Our tales (anag.)

indicators.note: the printed abbreviation instructs the solver to rearrange the letters of the words before it

explanation.surface: Some stories of ours, offered as a plain jumble.
explanation.walkthrough: An old-style clue with no definition at all: rearrange OUR TALES and confirm with crossing letters.
explanation.definitionFit: No definition is printed; the rearranged result is a botanical word for leaves arranged like a rosette.

clue.text: Alligator up a tree

parts.note: the fruit is also called the alligator pear, and it grows on a tree

explanation.surface: An absurd image of a reptile climbing a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Alligator pear' is another name for this fruit, so the 'alligator' hanging in a tree is the fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: The pear-shaped fruit is known as the alligator pear for its rough green skin, and it grows on trees.

clue.text: Joined by Browning with a bust

definitions.text: Joined by Browning with a bust

parts.words: Joined by Browning with a bust
parts.note: Robert Browning wrote a poem titled 'The ... and the Bust', pairing the answer with a bust

explanation.surface: Something linked by a man called Browning to a sculpted head.
explanation.walkthrough: Browning's poem 'The Statue and the Bust' joins the two in its title; a bust is also sculpture, so the pairing is apt.
explanation.definitionFit: Browning's poem title couples a carved figure with a bust, both pieces of sculpture.

clue.text: Set six poor interpreters to rights

indicators.note: to set something to rights is to put it in order, so the words set six poor are rearranged

explanation.surface: An instruction to correct six poor translators.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set ... to rights' reads as putting the six poor in order; the indicator is 'to rights' and SET SIX POOR is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: People who expound or explain texts are interpreters of them.

clue.text: Low-class salesman, all French

definitions.meaning: a pushy seller, such as one ... tickets outside a ground

explanation.surface: A cheap salesman who is entirely French.
explanation.definitionFit: A pushy street seller solicits trade, and the French word meaning all is spelt the same.

clue.text: Make an effort to get.. three points

definitions.meaning: in rugby, a touchdown over the line once scored three points

explanation.surface: Effort needed to score three points.
explanation.walkthrough: In rugby union, grounding the ball over the opponents' line was worth three points when this was set.
explanation.definitionFit: To attempt is to make an effort, and in rugby the grounding score was worth three points.

clue.text: A Benedictine

parts.note: a member of the French Benedictine congregation of St Maur, famed for scholarship

explanation.walkthrough: The Congregation of St Maur was a French Benedictine body noted for historical scholarship; a member takes his name from it.
explanation.definitionFit: The monks of the Congregation of St Maur were French Benedictines, so one of them is a Benedictine.

clue.text: No place for those who insist on themselves

definitions.text: No place for those who insist on themselves

parts.words: No place for those who insist on themselves
parts.note: the Buddhist state of bliss involves extinguishing the self, so the self-assertive are excluded

explanation.surface: A remark that egotists are unwelcome somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: In Buddhism the final blissful state is reached by extinguishing desire and the self, so egotists cannot get there.
explanation.definitionFit: The Buddhist goal of release is the extinction of the self, so it is no place for egotists.

clue.text: Ten days on without conjunctions

indicators.note: the setter prints no true anagram signal; this phrase, naming the figure of speech, is the only nudge that the words before it must be rearranged

explanation.surface: A period of ten days passing without meetings.
explanation.walkthrough: An old-style clue: TEN DAYS ON is rearranged with no real anagram indicator, and 'without conjunctions' serves as the definition. 'Conjunctions' looks like planetary meetings but means linking words such as 'and'.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhetorical term names the leaving out of linking words such as 'and' between clauses.

clue.text: " Do I carry the in my pocket?" (Browning)

definitions.text: " Do I carry the in my pocket?" (Browning)

parts.words: " Do I carry the in my pocket?" (Browning)
parts.note: a line from Browning's 'Master Hugues of Saxe-Gotha' with a word missing, supplied by the solver

explanation.surface: A quotation from Browning with a word left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: Browning's line asks 'Do I carry the moon in my pocket?', meaning he cannot do the impossible; the gap is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word in Browning's question is the heavenly body nobody could carry in a pocket.
